opus-5.5.text:
Coming out of academia, I think I had this belief, maybe a slightly naive one, that if you build the best technology, everything else follows. At OctoML we had a very strong technical foundation. Many of us came from the TVM project and the machine learning compilation community, and we were proud of the engineering. That excellence really mattered. It earned us credibility, it attracted great people, and it let us do things that were genuinely hard.

What I learned is that technical excellence is necessary but not sufficient. In a startup it's a means, not the end. The question isn't "is this the most elegant solution?" but "does this solve a problem someone urgently needs solved, right now, in a form they can actually adopt?" Sometimes the most technically interesting part of your stack isn't what customers care about at all. They care that it works, that it's easy to integrate, and that it fits how they already operate.

The landscape also shifted quickly. When we started, the big pain point was deploying models across many different hardware backends. Then generative AI arrived and the center of gravity moved toward serving large models efficiently, and the market started to consolidate around a few hardware platforms. We had to pivot, and that taught me that technical depth gives you options, but timing and focus decide which of those options become a business.

So my current view is that technical excellence works best as a compounding asset, the thing that lets you move faster and adapt when the world changes, rather than a moat by itself. You have to pair it with a very honest, continuous look at where the real demand is. That's also shaped how I think about research now. I still love working on deep systems problems, but I pay much more attention to how a piece of technology actually reaches people and creates value.

r001.rationale: The response discusses a market shift and pivot, but does not state that Octo would have lost badly by continuing to optimize ResNet along its original technical path.

r002.rationale: It says technical excellence is necessary but not sufficient and stresses customer demand, adoption, timing, and focus. It does not identify nontechnical execution as necessary to achieving technical excellence.

r003.rationale: The response says startup experience changed Tianqi’s view: technical excellence is a means rather than an end, and he now pays closer attention to how technology reaches people and creates value.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the honest answer is that my view on this changed quite a bit through OctoML, and the change was mostly about learning where technical excellence actually matters, rather than whether it matters.

Coming out of academia, with XGBoost and then TVM, my instinct was that if you build the best technology, the rest follows. And technical excellence is genuinely necessary. In machine learning systems especially, you cannot fake it. If your compiler produces slower code than the alternative, or your inference stack falls over under real traffic, users find out in about a week. There is no amount of marketing that saves you. So the baseline is that you have to be very good at the thing you claim to do.

But what Octo taught me is that being technically excellent is a necessary condition, not a sufficient one. The hard questions were almost never "can we make this run faster." We usually could. The hard questions were "faster for whom, on which hardware, delivered in what form, and does anyone's workflow actually change because of it." A startup lives or dies on whether the technology meets a real user at the right abstraction level and at the right moment. We spent time early on optimizing things that were technically impressive but that sat too far below where customers actually felt pain. The engineering was great. The strategic fit was not yet there.

The second thing I learned is about timing and compounding. The ML landscape moved incredibly fast during those years. We started in a world of many model architectures and many hardware targets, and then large language models collapsed a lot of that diversity. Suddenly the question was less about general compilation and more about serving a handful of very large models extremely well. Technical excellence in a startup has to be paired with the willingness to re-aim it quickly. The teams that did well were not the ones with the deepest single technique, but the ones that could redirect strong engineering toward the problem that had become urgent.

Third, I came to appreciate that technical excellence is itself a strategy for attracting people. The reason strong engineers joined was that they wanted to work on hard, real problems with people who took the craft seriously. That culture is a real asset, and it is one that a startup can build even before it has product-market fit. But you have to channel it. Excellence without direction turns into very polished solutions to problems nobody is asking you to solve.

The last piece, and this connects to how I think about open source, is that technical depth gives you optionality. Because we had built things like TVM as open ecosystems, the knowledge did not disappear when the market shifted. It flowed into other efforts, including the work I do now on bringing large models to run on all kinds of devices. A startup bet can be wrong in its timing and still produce technology that outlives it, if the work was done well and shared.

So my summary would be: technical excellence sets the floor, strategy sets the ceiling. You need the floor to be very high in this field, but you spend most of your actual effort as a founder figuring out where to point that excellence, and being honest with yourself about when the answer has changed.

astra-6.text:
I think technical excellence is essential, but it has to connect to something the customer actually cares about. As technical founders, we can get excited about making a system faster or solving a particularly difficult engineering problem. But that improvement only becomes a business advantage if it helps someone accomplish their goal—whether that means reducing cost, improving reliability, or making something easier to use.

My takeaway from Octo is that technical strategy and business strategy need to develop together. You need to ask not only, “Can we build this?” but also, “Who needs it, and why would they choose us?” Technical excellence gives you the ability to deliver. Understanding the customer helps you decide what is worth delivering.

sol-6.1.text:
My takeaway is that technical excellence has to serve a clear customer need. As engineers, we naturally want to solve the hardest problem or build the most elegant system. But in a startup, the question is whether that work helps someone enough that they will adopt the product and pay for it.

That doesn’t make technical depth less important. It means being deliberate about where you apply it. You need to understand which technical advantage really matters to the customer, prove that value quickly, and let what you learn shape the next investment. Technical excellence and business strategy have to reinforce each other.
